title: Financial modelling, part 5: debt, interest and circularity in a model
subtitle: Why interest expense creates a circular reference, and how to deal with it
whyItMatters: The interest circularity is the classic technical problem every model builder runs into. Understanding why it appears and how it can be handled is a clear marker separating people who have actually built models from people who have only read about them.
openingQuestion: Why does charging interest on the average debt balance create a circular reference?
openingOptions: Because Excel simply cannot handle a division that references itself
Because interest hits profit → cash → debt balance → back to interest
Because the debt balance always comes out negative in the model
Because the interest rate itself changes over the forecast
explanation: The chain of dependencies closes on itself: interest is charged on the average debt balance → interest reduces net profit → net profit affects cash flow → cash flow determines whether the company borrows more or repays → that changes the closing debt balance → which changes the average balance → which changes the interest. Excel spots a cell depending on itself and raises a circular reference error.

realWorldExample.description: In models with a revolving credit facility the circularity is close to unavoidable: the company draws more when it is short of cash and repays when it has surplus, and interest expense is itself part of that cash requirement. This is why many professional models have to enable iterative calculation or build in a switch to break the loop.

quiz.question: What is the simplest and safest way to handle the circularity?
options: Delete every interest expense formula from the forecast model
Raise Excel's maximum iteration count up to 1,000
Type the interest expense in by hand for each year
Charge interest on the opening balance, not the average
quiz.explanation: Using the opening balance severs the dependency chain, because the opening balance is already known and does not depend on anything happening during the period. It trades a small amount of precision for a large gain in stability. Deleting the interest line removes a real cost from the forecast, raising the iteration cap keeps the loop and just runs it longer, and hardcoding the figure buries an assumption inside the model.

quiz.question: What does enabling iterative calculation in Excel do?
options: Lets the calculation repeat until the result converges
Removes the circularity from the financial model entirely
Speeds up calculation in a large spreadsheet file
Automatically finds and fixes incorrect formulas
quiz.explanation: Excel repeats the calculation until the difference between two successive passes falls below a preset threshold. It solves the circularity but makes the model more fragile and harder to debug. Crucially it does not remove the loop - the loop is still there, merely tolerated. Nor does it help performance, and it has no capacity whatsoever to detect a formula that is simply wrong.

quiz.question: What is the risk of running a model with iterative calculation on?
options: No risk at all, provided the option is switched on properly
It may fail to converge and spread errors model-wide
The file locks and can no longer be edited at all
Excel rewrites the user's formulas into another form
quiz.explanation: A circularity makes errors propagate and become hard to trace. Many institutions ban iterative calculation outright and require models to be designed without any loop at all. The setting does not lock the file or alter anyone's formulas - what it changes is that the numbers on screen may quietly stop reflecting the current assumptions, with no warning of any kind.

quiz.question: What role does a revolver play in a model?
options: Records extra equity contributed by existing shareholders
Calculates depreciation on newly purchased fixed assets
A regulating valve: draw when short, repay when in surplus
Forecasts revenue for each year covered by the model
quiz.explanation: The revolver keeps the cash balance from ever falling below a safe minimum, which is how businesses genuinely manage short-term liquidity. It is a debt facility, so it has nothing to do with equity contributions, nothing to do with the fixed asset schedule where depreciation is computed, and nothing to do with revenue, which is an input assumption rather than a plug.

quiz.question: Which fix for the interest circularity is safest in a model others will reuse?
options: Type in each year's interest by hand from a rough first estimate
Turn on iteration in Excel and set a large enough iteration cap
Run a macro that recalculates the whole model until it converges
Charge interest on the opening debt balance to cut the loop
quiz.explanation: Interest on the opening balance differs slightly from interest on the average balance, but it eliminates entirely the risk of the model producing garbage when someone opens the file without iteration enabled. For a model that has to pass through many hands, that trade is almost always worth making. A hardcoded figure stops responding to the scenario, and a macro adds a dependency the next user may never run.

keyTakeaways: The circularity arises when interest is charged on the average balance, because interest feeds back into that very balance
The safest fix: charge interest on the OPENING balance, severing the dependency chain
Iterative calculation resolves the loop but makes the model fragile and hard to debug
The revolver is the regulating valve that keeps cash from falling below its minimum

practicePrompt.question: Your model reports a circular reference after you added the interest expense line. You are presenting to the leadership team in 30 minutes. What is the most sensible thing to do?
options: Turn on iterative calculation and hope the model converges in time
Charge interest on the opening debt balance to drop the loop
Delete the interest line so the model runs at all
Type in an estimated interest figure for each year
practicePrompt.explanation: Switching to the opening balance is clean, immediate and transparent: the loop is gone, results are stable, and the difference against the average-balance method is usually negligible at the level of the decision being made. What matters is documenting the choice clearly in the assumptions. Deleting the interest line or hardcoding it both hide the problem, and enabling iteration right before a meeting is a risk you do not need to take.

summary.keyIdea: Interest creates a circularity because it is both an output and an input of the debt balance
summary.commonMistake: Enabling iterative calculation without understanding the risk, leaving the model producing unstable results.
summary.action: Try building a simple debt schedule and deliberately create the circularity to see how Excel reacts.

application.title: Experiment with the circularity
application.message: Build a three-year debt schedule with interest on the average balance and watch Excel raise the error. Then switch to the opening balance and compare the two results so you can judge the size of the difference for yourself.
application.secondary: Knowing the real size of that difference lets you defend your design choice with confidence.

sections.text: The circular reference is the error that confuses new model builders most, because a model that was running perfectly suddenly reports an error the moment you add one apparently harmless line: interest expense.

items: Interest is charged on the average debt balance for the period
Interest is an expense, so it reduces net profit
Net profit affects operating cash flow
Cash flow determines whether the business borrows more or repays
The closing debt balance changes → the average balance changes → back to step 1

left.label: Interest on the average balance
left.text: More accurate in financial terms, but it creates the circularity and needs iterative calculation.

right.label: Interest on the opening balance
right.text: A small error, but the loop is severed completely. Many institutions make this their default purely for the stability.

sections.label: A trade-off worth weighing
sections.text: The extra accuracy from the average-balance method is usually tiny next to the inherent error in the revenue assumptions. Trading a little accuracy for stability and debuggability is usually the right call - as long as you document it clearly.
How small the real difference is

Opening debt 100bn, another 20bn drawn during the year, interest rate 10%. On the opening balance: interest = 10bn. On the average balance of (100 + 120)/2 = 110: interest = 11bn. That is a 1bn difference at a business with pre-tax profit in the hundreds of billions - below the noise in the revenue assumption itself, which is typically off by several percent. That is the entire price of severing the loop. In return, the model always produces the same result from the same set of assumptions, and anyone opening the file can trace from cell to cell without ending up going in a circle.

sections.title: Three ways to handle it, and what each one costs
sections.subtitle: Ordered by how safe they are once the model is reused by someone else

concepts.def: Severs the loop at its source. The error sits below the noise in the assumptions. The default choice at most investment banks, and the only one that stays auditable by eye.

Excel solves it approximately by running repeated passes until two successive ones differ by less than a threshold. It preserves the average-balance method, but the result depends on the starting value, and a single error cell anywhere leaves the whole model frozen on its previous numbers with no notice.
An on/off cell that forces interest to zero to break the loop while debugging, then switches back. Used alongside iteration; it is not a substitute for it.

sections.label: Why enabling iteration right before a meeting is a risk
sections.text: Iteration converges on an approximate solution rather than a unique one - change the calculation order, or open the file on another machine with a different threshold, and the numbers shift slightly. Worse: when a #REF! or #DIV/0! appears anywhere in the model, Excel stops iterating and keeps the results of the previous pass, so the schedule still shows presentable numbers while it has stopped reflecting the current assumptions. Nothing warns you. If you must use it, put in a check cell comparing the two sides of the balance sheet and flag it red when they diverge.

lines: The circularity is not an Excel bug - it reflects a genuine causal relationship in finance.
